title: The Safe Behind The Ring
text:
The Safe Behind The Ring
A practice brief for Action: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Loading Bay
The Safe Behind The Ring

A boxing coach locking up late finds the best student she ever trained prying open the office safe, and has to get him out of her gym empty-handed without either of them getting hurt.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A small boxing gym above a hardware store, at eleven at night, the ring lights off and only the office lamp on. The safe holds a month of members’ dues, this month’s rent among them. He owes money to men who don’t wait, and he came on the one night she was meant to be at her sister’s.
The Two Of You
Coach and pupil for eight years: she found him at fourteen picking fights outside the station. He walked out after a loss last spring and hasn’t answered her calls since.
You Play
Coach Imelda Ruiz, fifty-four, a former featherweight champion with a shoulder that never healed right.
The Reader Plays
Teo, twenty-three, her best student once, hood up, crouched at the safe just off frame.
How They Play It
Pressing: playing opposite it, the tape counts responsiveness for more and leans on your adaptability.
The Genre Asks
Command Of The Frame: Status and threat carried in the body and the look more than the words: the person everyone in the room watches. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and execution, and calls on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.
Suspense Held: A threat kept alive under every line: what’s at stake never dropped, even in the quiet. A self-tape in it is judged more on consistency and interpretation, and calls on your focus and listening and responsiveness. The breakdown, then rehearsal: suspense is held by knowing at every moment what your character fears will happen, and keeping it alive through the scene.
Its chases and fights are staged techniques; between them the scenes turn on who holds the frame and what the threat is. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Make him drop the pry bar and go down the front stairs with his pockets empty.
What’s In The Way
He’s younger and faster, he knows which shoulder is the bad one, and he fears the men he owes more than he fears her.
WHERE IT TURNS
She switches on the ring lights and says his name, and he doesn’t stop working at the lock. (Grave)
She talks about his first amateur bout, the one he won on a split decision, to keep him listening. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)
He rushes her to reach the stairs; the fight is four marked moves, and the first one catches her bad shoulder. (Grave)
She slips his last swing and has him beaten, her right hand cocked, and she doesn’t throw it. (Grave)
He tells her who he owes and how much, and she laughs, because it’s less than the new roof cost. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
She opens the safe herself, counts the debt out onto the desk, and tells him he starts sweeping the gym at six tomorrow. (Lyric)

4 changes of tone between beats and 2 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. A slow start in the half dark, a memory used to hold him, a fight she wins by not finishing it, then a laugh and a debt paid in work.

WHAT THE SAFE BEHIND THE RING ASKS
Everyday Speech, on camera
Timing: Much. The fight’s four moves sit inside the talk, and each move cuts off the line before it, so you have to place exactly where the words stop.
Physical Work: Built On It. She plays the scene in a body that still knows how to fight and a shoulder that can’t: the stance, the four moves, the punch held back, all on her side of the frame.
Playing Off The Partner: Built On It. She reads him the way she read him from the corner, and every turn of the scene answers something he does or says.
Vocal Demand: Some
Tone: grave to lyric to comic, 4 transitions to play. A slow start in the half dark, a memory used to hold him, a fight she wins by not finishing it, then a laugh and a debt paid in work.
Techniques It Asks: Stage Combat. The fight is staged combat. Mark its four moves solo, at reduced speed, against the reader’s called cues from off camera, with no contact. React to the hit on her shoulder; it never lands. The pry bar stays off frame with him and is only talked about.

title: The Spillway Walk
text:
The Spillway Walk
A practice brief for Anime: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Last Launch From The Roof
The Spillway Walk

In an anime dub, a young dam keeper holds a jammed flood gate shut by hand while she talks her little brother across the narrow walkway below it.

THE SCENE
Where And When
You record alone at a microphone against finished picture: a mountain town’s old stone dam in a storm, each line cued by bars that run across the frame. In the story the gate’s motor has broken down, and the keeper is turning the hand wheel to hold it shut while her brother, who followed her out, is halfway across the spillway walk under it. Each line and each effort sound has to sit on the drawn mouth and the drawn strain.
The Two Of You
Sister and brother, eight years apart. Since their mother left, she has raised him, and he follows her everywhere.
You Play
Sayo, nineteen, apprentice dam keeper, holding the wheel with everything she has.
You Speak To
Kenta, her brother, eleven, already recorded on the track. Play against his lines and his frightened breathing in your headphones.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
Dense Text, Exact: A lot of words, or difficult ones, delivered fluently and at speed: jargon, argument or deduction as second nature. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and interpretation, and calls on your memory and focus. Learning the lines: fluency at speed is the lines learned past knowing them.
Dubbing asks for emotional truth sized to the drawn image while the timing fits mouth movements that already exist. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Keep him walking and keep him calm until he reaches the far side.
What’s In The Way
The wheel is slipping, he freezes whenever he looks down, and every word has to land on drawings that won’t wait for her.
WHERE IT TURNS
She tells him to look at her and not at the water, her voice steady over the strain of the wheel. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)
The wheel slips a turn; her effort sounds land on the drawn strain, and the lines come out between breaths. (Grave)
She makes him laugh with their old joke about their mother’s cooking, to get his feet moving again. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
He reaches the far rail, and she lets the wheel go with a shout, half a laugh and half a sob, as the gate gives way behind him. (Lyric and Comic, held at once)

3 changes of tone between beats and 3 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Calm laid over strain, a slip that tests it, a joke to get him moving, then the release.

WHAT THE SPILLWAY WALK ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Much. Each line sits on cue bars and drawn mouths, and the effort sounds have to fit the drawn strain on the wheel to the frame.
Physical Work: Some
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Built On It. She shouts over a storm, strains at the wheel and keeps her voice gentle for him, all at once and for the length of the scene: a long, hard demand on the voice.
Tone: grave to lyric to comic, 3 transitions to play. Calm laid over strain, a slip that tests it, a joke to get him moving, then the release.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. It’s a dub, recorded alone at a microphone to finished animation and her brother’s recorded lines, so match the effort sounds to the picture as well as the words. Play the struggle with the wheel in your breath, and keep your body still at the microphone.

title: The Last Thing Handed In
text:
The Last Thing Handed In
A practice brief for Anthology: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Seat Fourteen
The Last Thing Handed In

The narrator who opens and closes every story in an anthology film set at a railway lost-property office reaches the last one, and the object handed in is one she lost herself.

THE SCENE
Where And When
An anthology film of six stories, each beginning when an object is handed in at a railway lost-property office and ending when its owner claims it. The same unseen narrator opens and closes each one in four rhymed lines. This is the last story: the object is a child’s red glove, and the narrator lost it on a platform forty years ago and has kept its pair ever since.
The Two Of You
Until now the narrator has never been a character in the film; the audience knows only her voice, and the glove is the first thing in six stories that belongs to her.
You Play
The narrator, a woman in her fifties whose name the film never gives.
You Speak To
The audience, as in the five stories before, and in the close, the glove on the counter.
The Genre Asks
Played Straight: Meant completely: the feeling played with full conviction, never winked at, however large or strange the material. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and connection, and calls on your emotional depth and presence. The breakdown and the lines: believing it starts with knowing exactly what your character wants and why it matters to them.
A form, not a style: each segment is a drama, played truthfully in a few minutes. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Open and close the last story in the voice she has used for every other one.
What’s In The Way
The glove is hers, the rhymes written for her say so plainly, and her voice wants to change.
WHERE IT TURNS
The familiar opening: the office, the counter, the glove handed in, spoken as evenly as the five before. (Lyric)
The close: she names the glove as hers, and lets the even voice give way for a single line before she finishes the film. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)

1 change of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. A familiar opening, then a close in which the story turns out to be the narrator’s own.

WHAT THE LAST THING HANDED IN ASKS
Verse: The narrator speaks in rhymed lines, four to open each story and four to close it, and the rhyme has to hold when her voice doesn’t.
Timing: Much. The narration is laid over picture, and each couplet has to end where the cut does.
Vocal Demand: Much. Hold one even narrating voice through the opening, then let it give for a single line in the close, all of it carried on the breath.
Tone: lyric to grave, 1 transition to play. A familiar opening, then a close in which the story turns out to be the narrator’s own.
Techniques It Asks: Classical Text. Speaking rhymed verse to its meter over finished picture asks for classical text work.
It Only Takes: Set. Every story opens and closes in the same rhymed shape, and the scene depends on the last one matching the others. It can only be played set, the same way every time.

title: The Night Register
text:
The Night Register
A practice brief for Exploitation: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
Closed For The Season
The Night Register

At a highway motel in 1977, the night clerk hides a runaway from the commune’s recruiter, and has to get through the slow dance he asks her for without giving the girl away.

THE SCENE
Where And When
The office of a motel off a two-lane highway in the pine country, past midnight in July 1977, with a jukebox beside the counter for the truckers. A girl of seventeen walked out of the farm commune up the valley this afternoon and is asleep in room 9. The man who brings the commune its new members has come down to look for her, and two more of them wait in his van.
The Two Of You
He stops at the motel every few weeks, tips too well, and has always liked her more than she liked him.
You Play
Lou Ann Pruitt, thirty, the night clerk, chewing gum, with the register under the counter and the jukebox at her elbow.
The Reader Plays
Brother Caleb, the recruiter, smiling, in a white shirt, leaning on the counter.
How They Play It
Pressing: playing opposite it, the tape counts responsiveness for more and leans on your adaptability.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
States At The Limit: Fear, grief or exhaustion at their extreme, sustained, and believed though the threat is often not in the room. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and execution, and calls on your emotional depth and physical expression. The lines, then rehearsal on your feet: an extreme state has to be found in the body, on lines you no longer think about.
Shot in days, sold on sensation that its performers supplied at full size. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Keep him away from the register and out of room 9 until he gives up and drives off.
What’s In The Way
He’s charming and patient, his friends are waiting in the van, and he asks her to dance so he can read her face up close.
WHERE IT TURNS
He asks to see the register, all smiles; she plays bored, chews her gum and talks about the heat. (Comic and Grotesque, held at once)
He asks her to put a song on and dance with him, and she can’t refuse without telling him something; she drops a coin in the jukebox, and in the slow dance he talks softly about the girl and watches her eyes. (Lyric and Grotesque, held at once)
Halfway through the song he guesses room 9 out loud, and she laughs at him and keeps dancing. (Comic and Grotesque, held at once)
The song ends; she tells him the girl hitched a ride north an hour ago, and holds his eye until he believes her. (Grave)

3 changes of tone between beats and 3 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Boredom played to keep him out, a dance he uses to search her face, a right guess she laughs off, then the lie as the music stops.

WHAT THE NIGHT REGISTER ASKS
Everyday Speech, on camera
Timing: Much. The song is the clock: she has to keep her face still for as long as it plays, and the lie lands as the music stops.
Physical Work: Much. The slow dance is the scene’s center: a set of choreographed moves held through dialogue. Dance it solo toward his eyeline beside the lens, with the jukebox on your side of the frame. He leads, and she keeps her face still at the distance he chooses.
Playing Off The Partner: Built On It. He’s pressing the whole time, and she has to judge from his guesses how near the truth he’s getting.
Tone: comic to grotesque to lyric to grave, 3 transitions to play. Boredom played to keep him out, a dance he uses to search her face, a right guess she laughs off, then the lie as the music stops.
Techniques It Asks: Intimacy. The slow dance is staged intimacy, agreed in advance with an intimacy coordinator and played solo. Sway in a hold around no one toward his eyeline, never touching the reader, the same on every take. None of it is explicit: the closeness is his, used to read her.

text:
The Enchanted Folding Chair
A practice brief for Slapstick: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Last Strip
The Enchanted Folding Chair

A father picked as the volunteer at his daughter’s seventh birthday magic show is betrayed by every prop the magician tells him to pick up.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A rented party room behind a roller rink on a Saturday afternoon, fourteen seven-year-olds cross-legged on the floor and paper plates of cake waiting on a side table. The magician’s assistant went home sick, so she picked Gil from the parents to help. He promised his daughter this would be the best party of the year. For the tape, the props wait on a low table on your side of the frame, the magician’s voice comes from beside the lens, and a crash mat lies hidden behind the little chair.
The Two Of You
Strangers. The magician needs a volunteer with a sense of humor and has decided, at a glance, that Gil has one.
You Play
Gil Esposito, forty, an insurance adjuster, careful by trade, who badly wants his daughter to be proud of him.
The Reader Plays
The Amazing Delphine, the magician, who calls the next trick before he’s finished the last and changes their order every time.
How They Play It
Unpredictable: playing opposite it, the tape counts responsiveness and consistency for more and leans on your adaptability and composure.
The Genre Asks
Comic Rhythm: Setup and payoff: cues picked up, pauses placed, the laugh landing where the timing puts it. A self-tape in it is judged more on responsiveness and execution, and calls on your adaptability and focus. Rehearsing on your feet: timing lives in the exchange and is found by playing it through.
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
The slapstick comic is acrobat and stunt performer, with perfect timing. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Get through every trick looking as if he meant it, for his daughter in the front row.
What’s In The Way
Every prop is rigged to fail on the volunteer, the magician improvises the order, and fourteen children laugh hardest when he gets hurt.
WHERE IT TURNS
Told to tie the magic rope, he watches it fall apart in his hands in six pieces, and bows as if that were the trick. (Comic)
Told to sit on the enchanted chair, a child’s folding chair, he feels it fold under him and goes over backward. (Comic and Grotesque, held at once)
Told to tap the top hat with the wand, he watches the wand droop, and the hat springs up off the table into his nose. (Comic)
He finds his daughter’s face in the front row, fixes the broken wand with enormous ceremony, and it stays broken; he takes his bow anyway. (Lyric and Comic, held at once)

3 changes of tone between beats and 2 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Three gags that climb from embarrassment to a fall to a hit, then a bow that’s funny and tender at once.

WHAT THE ENCHANTED FOLDING CHAIR ASKS
Everyday Speech, on camera
Timing: Built On It. Each gag lands on the magician’s call, and the calls never come in the same order twice.
Physical Work: Built On It. A rope that falls apart, a fall backward off a folding chair, a hat that springs into his face and a grand bow: the scene is a body betrayed by objects.
Playing Off The Partner: Built On It. Every trick starts on the magician’s call, and he has to take each one as it comes and play it back to her.
Vocal Demand: Some
Freedom To Improvise: Some
Tone: comic to grotesque to lyric, 3 transitions to play. Three gags that climb from embarrassment to a fall to a hit, then a bow that’s funny and tender at once.
Techniques It Asks: Clown And Mask, Stage Combat, Comedy. The rope, the hat and the wand are slapstick’s clowning, and they ask for comic timing. text:
The Hammer Spring
A practice brief for Western: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Well At Cutbank
The Hammer Spring

A gunsmith in a cattle town is asked to mend a young cowhand’s revolver in time for the gunfight he has agreed to at sundown, and has an hour to decide whether to fix it.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A gunsmith’s shop on the main street of a Kansas cattle town in the summer of 1878, late afternoon. Last night in the saloon a hired gun goaded the boy into a challenge, and half the town heard him accept. His late father’s revolver has a broken hammer spring, and the spring that would mend it lies in her drawer. For the tape, the revolver is an unloaded replica, and it never leaves your side of the counter.
The Two Of You

You Play

The Genre Asks

A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and execution, and calls on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.
Feeling Held In: The feeling is there and kept under: stillness, economy, what isn’t said carrying what is. A self-tape in it is judged more on consistency and believability, and calls on your composure and focus. Learning the lines and rehearsing on your feet: control comes from knowing it well enough to hold it still.
Cowboy camps teach riding and guns; the western’s hero says little and owns the frame. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.

title: Episode Two Hundred
text:
Episode Two Hundred
A practice brief for Tragicomedy: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Three Minutes
Episode Two Hundred

Recording alone, a radio host makes the last episode of the comedy show she made with her late partner for eleven years, playing both halves of their oldest running bit.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A small studio at a community radio station on a Sunday night. For eleven years Bea and Lou made a weekly comedy show for the station; Lou died in the summer, and the station asked Bea for one last episode for the listeners. Their oldest bit was an argument between two neighbors over a fence, Bea as one and Lou as the other. Tonight she plays both. You record it alone at a microphone, live to tape, as the episode goes out.
The Two Of You
Partners on air for eleven years and friends for thirty; off the air they argued about everything, on it only about the fence.
You Play
Bea Rourke, sixty-two, quick, dry and set on getting through it without the listeners hearing her cry.
You Speak To
The listeners, and in the bit, each neighbor to the other. There’s no reader.
The Genre Asks
Comic Rhythm: Setup and payoff: cues picked up, pauses placed, the laugh landing where the timing puts it. A self-tape in it is judged more on responsiveness and execution, and calls on your adaptability and focus. Rehearsing on your feet: timing lives in the exchange and is found by playing it through.
Played Straight: Meant completely: the feeling played with full conviction, never winked at, however large or strange the material. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and connection, and calls on your emotional depth and presence. The breakdown and the lines: believing it starts with knowing exactly what your character wants and why it matters to them.
Tone shifting between the serious and the comic, often within a scene. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Give the listeners the show Lou would have wanted, and get to the end of it.
What’s In The Way
The bit was built for two voices and two kinds of timing, Lou’s half is the funnier, and every line of it is his.
WHERE IT TURNS
She opens the show as always: the theme hummed, the weather, and a complaint about the station’s coffee. (Comic)
She says, briefly and without fuss, that Lou won’t be on tonight. (Grave)

In Lou’s voice, his neighbor says the line he always ended on, and she can’t answer it in her own. (Comic and Grave, held at once)

title: Column Nine
text:
Column Nine
A practice brief for Alternate History: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
The Receiver
Column Nine

In a world where a treaty outlawed the electronic computer before the first one was finished, the head of a forecast hall where two hundred people compute the weather by hand finds an error ninety minutes before a storm warning must go out, and talks the whole hall through the work again over the loudspeaker.

THE SCENE
Where And When
The forecast hall of the national weather service in 1969, in a world where a treaty signed in 1946 forbade any machine that calculates electronically, and none was ever built. Two hundred people at tiered desks work tomorrow’s weather by hand and by mechanical adding machine, one patch of map each, and the head of the hall speaks to them from a gallery microphone. A storm is coming up the coast, and the warning has to reach the radio stations by six. At half past four she finds that column nine, the southern pressure figures, carried a wrong number from the first sheet. You record alone at a microphone, and the hall is only on screen.
The Two Of You
She came up through the desks herself and knows most of the two hundred by their handwriting. They trust her voice more than any memo from upstairs.
You Play
Odile Brandt, fifty, head of the forecast hall, twenty-six years on its floor and its gallery.
You Speak To
The hall’s two hundred computers, the people at the desks below the gallery. Their figures come up to you on paper slips, and none of them is in the booth.
The Genre Asks
Another Age’s Manners: How people of another time stood, moved, spoke and kept their place, kept up without looking like effort. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and interpretation, and calls on your physical expression, discipline and vocal expression. The breakdown and rehearsal together: the manners are researched first, then made habit on your feet.
Belief In What Isn’t There: An invented world made concrete: the creature, the machine or the magic played as specifically as a cup of tea. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and interpretation, and calls on your imagination. The breakdown: the world’s rules have to be worked out before they can be believed.
A past that didn’t happen: another age’s manners, and a world changed by one event, both to be made concrete. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Get the corrected column worked, checked and out to the radio stations by six, without the hall losing its nerve.
What’s In The Way
Ninety minutes is barely enough to work the column once, the hall has been at it since dawn, and every person down there will hear in her voice how wrong the warning would have been.
WHERE IT TURNS
She gives the afternoon announcement as on any storm day, with the dry joke about the coffee that the hall expects from her. (Comic)
She stops the hall: column nine is wrong from the first sheet, and every desk south of the river has to work it again. (Grave)
She talks them through the new order of work, desk by desk, each figure read twice and slow enough to be written down. (Grave)
At twenty to six one desk’s figure disagrees with the check; she reads both out to the hall and asks them to find which is true. (Grave)
The checked forecast comes up, and she reads the warning to the hall before it goes out, then the name of every desk leader for the record. (Lyric)

The Song For Act Two

Three days before a musical comedy opens, its songwriter sings and dances the second act’s new opening number herself for a producer who hasn’t smiled in twenty years, because the chorus has quit and the song is needed by morning.

THE SCENE
Where And When
An empty rehearsal hall over a dance school in 1934, at one in the morning, with an upright piano and a pianist hired by the hour.
